Chapter 1
Template
1.1 How to compile a .tex ﬁle to a .pdf ﬁle
1.1.1 Tools
To process the ﬁles you (may) need:
• pdflatex (for example from tetex package≥0.9-6, which you can
get from Red Hat 5.2);
• acroread (a PDF viewer, available from http://www.adobe.com/);
• ghostscript≥5.10 (for example fromRed Hat Contrib) andghostview
orgv (from RedHat Linux);
• efax package could be useful, if you plan to fax documents.
1.1.2 How to use the tools
Follow these steps:
1. put all source.tex ﬁles in one directory, then chdir to the directory (or put
some of them in the LATEXsearch path — if you know how to do this);
2. run “pdflatex file.tex” on the main ﬁle of the document three times
(three — to prepare valid table of contents);
3. to see or print the result use acroread (unfortunately some versions of
acroread may produce PostScript which is too complex), or
5
6 CHAPTER 1. TEMPLATE
4. runghostscript: “gv file.pdf” to display or:
“gs -dNOPAUSE -sDEVICE=pswrite -q -dBATCH -sOutputFile=ﬁle.ps ﬁle.pdf”
to produce a PostScript ﬁle;
5. run “fax send phone-number file.ps” as root to send a fax, or — if you
know how to do this — modify the fax script to be able to fax.pdf ﬁles directly
(you have to insert “|%PDF*” somewhere. . . ).
1.2 How to write a document
1.2.1 The main document
Choose the name of the document, say document. Copy template.tex to
document.tex, then edit it, change the title, the authors and set proper in-
clude(s) for all the chapters.
1.2.2 Chapters
Each chapter should be included in the main document as a separate ﬁle. You can
choose any name for the ﬁle, but we suggest adding a sufﬁx to the name of the
main ﬁle. For our example we use the ﬁle name document_chapter1.tex.
First, copy template_chapter.tex to document_chapter1.tex
and add the line
\include{document_chapter1}
in thedocument.tex, then editdocument_chapter1.tex, change the
chapter title and edit the body of the chapter appropriately.
1.2.3 Spell-checking
Do use a spell-checker, please!
You may also want to check grammar, style and so on. Actually you should
do it (if you have enough spare time). But you must check spelling!
You can use the ispell package for this, from within emacs, or from the
command line:
ispell -t document_chapter1.tex
1.3. LATEX AND PDFLATEX CAPABILITIES 7
1.3 L ATEX and pdfLATEX capabilities
1.3.1 Overview
First you edit your source .tex ﬁle. In LATEX you compile it using the latex
command to a .dvi ﬁle (which stands for device-independent). The .dvi ﬁle
can be converted to any device-dependent format you like using an appropriate
driver, for exampledvips.
When producing .pdf ﬁles you should use pdflatex, which produces di-
rectly.pdf ﬁles out of .tex sources. Note that in the .tex ﬁle you may need
to use some PDF speciﬁc packages.
For viewing.tex ﬁles use your favourite text editor, for viewing .dvi ﬁles
under X Window System use xdvi command,.ps ﬁles can be viewed with gv
(orghostview) and.pdf ﬁles with acroread,gv orxpdf.
1.3.2 L ATEX
A lot of examples can be found in this document.
You should also print
• doc/latex/general/latex2e.dvi and
• doc/latex/general/lshort2e.dvi
from yourtetex distribution (usually in
• /usr/share/texmf or
• /usr/lib/texmf/texmf).
1.3.3 pdfL ATEX
Consult doc/pdftex/manual.pdf from your tetex distribution for more
details. Very useful informations can be found in thehyperref andgraphics
package manuals:
• doc/latex/hyperref/manual.pdf and
• doc/latex/graphics/grfguide.dvi.
1.3.4 Examples
References

2026-10-07 18:10:57: task_name="explainer", task="explain in the detail manner what is GPU Kernel ?.", agent="Developer", status="completed", output="### Short, Simple Answer
A **GPU Kernel** is a specialized function designed to run in parallel across thousands of small, efficient processor cores on a Graphics Processing Unit (GPU). While a standard CPU function typically executes one instruction on one piece of data at a time, a GPU kernel takes a single set of instructions and applies them to a massive collection of data points simultaneously.

---

### Detailed Technical Explanation

To understand a GPU kernel, we must first understand the fundamental difference between how a CPU and a GPU process information.

#### 1. The Architectural Context: Latency vs. Throughput
*   **CPU (Latency Oriented):** A CPU is designed to minimize the time it takes to complete a single sequence of complex tasks. It has a few powerful cores with large caches and sophisticated logic to handle branching (if/else statements) and complex instruction sets.
*   **GPU (Throughput Oriented):** A GPU is designed to maximize the amount of work done in a given window of time. It sacrifices complex logic and large individual caches for a massive number of simpler cores. It is built for "data parallelism"—performing the same mathematical operation on millions of pixels or numbers at once.

**The Kernel is the bridge between your code and this massive parallel hardware.**

#### 2. The Execution Model: SIMT
GPU kernels operate on a model known as **SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads)**. 

When you "launch" a kernel, you aren't just calling a function once. You are telling the GPU: *"Take this specific function (the kernel) and run it many thousands of times at once, but give each run its own unique piece of data."*

#### 3. The Hierarchy of Parallelism
To manage thousands of simultaneous executions, GPUs organize work into a specific hierarchy. If you write a kernel, you must define how it fits into this structure:

1.  **Thread:** The smallest unit of execution. A single thread executes the kernel code once for a single data element (e.g., one pixel in an image).
2.  **Block (or Work-group):** A collection of threads that are grouped together. Threads within the same block can communicate with each other and share a very fast, tiny piece of memory (called *Shared Memory*).
3.  **Grid:** The highest level of organization. A grid is the collection of all blocks launched to execute a specific kernel.

**Analogy:** 
Imagine you are a manager (the CPU) and you have a massive task: painting 1,000,000 tiny dots on a wall.
*   The **Kernel** is the "Instruction Manual" (e.g., "Dip brush in paint, press against wall, move to next dot").
*   The **Threads** are the individual workers.
*   The **Blocks** are teams of workers sharing a single bucket of paint (Shared Memory).
*   The **Grid** is the entire workforce assigned to the wall.

#### 4. Anatomy of a Kernel (Example in Pseudo-CUDA)
In a programming language like CUDA (used for NVIDIA GPUs), a kernel is defined using a special keyword (like `__global__`). 

Here is a conceptual example of a kernel that adds two arrays together:

```cpp
// The '__global__' keyword tells the compiler this function runs on the GPU
__global__ void vectorAdd(float* A, float* B, float* C, int n) {
    
    // Each thread calculates its own unique index using built-in variables
    // 'blockIdx' is which block we are in, 'threadIdx' is our position in that block
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;

    // Boundary check: ensure we don't access memory outside the array size
    if (i < n) {
        // Every thread performs this same math, but on different 'i' values
        C[i] = A[i] + B[i];
    }
}
```

**What is happening here?**
1.  **The Launch:** The CPU calls this function and tells the GPU, "Run this with a grid of 10,000 blocks."
2.  **The Parallelism:** Instead of a `for` loop running from `0` to `n`, the hardware spawns thousands of threads. 
3.  **The Indexing:** The line `int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;` is critical. It allows each thread to "know" which specific element of the array it is responsible for. This is how the same code handles different data.

#### 5. Key Constraints and Challenges
While kernels are incredibly fast, they come with specific engineering challenges:
*   **Branch Divergence:** If you put an `if/else` statement inside a kernel and half the threads go one way while the other half go the other, the GPU hardware often has to run both paths sequentially, which kills performance.
*   **Memory Latency:** Moving data from the system RAM (CPU side) to the VRAM (GPU side) is slow. A kernel is only effective if the computation it performs is heavy enough to justify the cost of moving the data.
*   **Memory Coalescing:** For maximum speed, threads in a block should access adjacent memory addresses so the hardware can "batch" the memory requests together.

### Summary Table
| Feature | CPU Function | GPU Kernel |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Execution** | Sequential (one after another) | Parallel (many at once) |
| **Goal** | Low Latency (fast single task) | High Throughput (massive data) |
| **Control Logic** | Very complex (branch prediction) | Very simple (minimal branching) |
| **Scaling** | Scales by increasing clock speed | Scales by increasing thread count |"

In traditional programming on a CPU, instructions are generally executed sequentially (one after another).
